claims.quote: 12:17 p.m. — I wrote the new observations into my notebook the way habit had taught me, the same habit that had me write "11:07 — silver locket. E.L." earlier.
claims.value: timestamps and records events in notebook

claims.quote: 11:27 a.m. — in my bedroom I propped the sepia photograph against the cracked mirror and let raking light coax the back into view. The ink was faint and smeared; under the light the letters resolved. On my phone screen it read, as legible as the smear allowed, "Oct 12 1913."

11:34 a.m. — I laid the locket beside the diary page I'd photographed in the attic and took close-ups. The letters on the silver were shallow and crude; in my photographs the inscription appeared to read E.L.

I sat on a joist and read the torn fragment aloud, careful to say it exactly as it lay: "—spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell." Those four words fit like a key and the rest of the page fell into a context I could map: "Oct 12 — tea and the clock. The clock stopped at four and twenty-two when Mam went for sugar."
claims.value: "—spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell."

claims.quote: 11:44 a.m. — In the light the stain read the colour of old tea — a bruised brown with speckled edges and a dry, stubborn skin.
11:18 a.m. — the hands sat at four twenty-two. The photograph saved as 2026-03-03_clock_4-22_front.jpg.
"Children left long ago," she said, clipped. Her fingers found a jar of preserves and slid it to the side like a small shield. "This house has its ways. We don't keep much past what's necessary."
